challenges.name: warm-up-evidence
challenges.title: Warm-up: read the windows before you compare
challenges.description: Two statements on the per-window p95 of a load test that started on freshly deployed pods, and on a comparison with a second run started on the same pods after it.

questions.question:
Run A: k6, constant arrival rate of 200 req/s on GET /api/leaderboard, started 40 s after a deploy replaced every API pod. The p95 of each 30 s window (computed from the raw samples, nearest-rank):

window     0-30s  30-60s  60-90s  90-120s  120-150s  150-180s  180-210s  210-240s
p95 (ms)     912     388     204      131       126       129       124       127
requests   5,980   6,010   6,002    5,995     6,004     5,998     6,001     6,003

k6 summary for the whole run: http_req_duration p(95)=371ms

Statement: "Reported as the p95 of the leaderboard, the 371 ms of the summary would mostly describe the first two windows: from 90 s on, every window's p95 is between 124 and 131 ms."
questions.explanation: True. The windows hold about the same number of requests, so the whole-run p95 is the value with 5% of all 48,000 samples above it, about 2,400 samples. The first two windows alone have enough slow requests (cold caches, empty connection pools, unoptimised code paths after a restart) to fill most of that top 5%, which drags the whole-run p95 up to 371 ms although six of eight windows sit between 124 and 131 ms. The misconception is that a whole-run percentile is a stable property of the service: it depends on how much warm-up the run happened to contain. Report the warm-up and the steady state separately.

questions.question:
Same pods as run A above. Right after run A finished, a developer deployed nothing, enabled a new cache flag for the leaderboard query through the admin API, and started run B with the same k6 script and rate.

run      whole-run p95   p95 of windows from 90 s on
A        371 ms          124-131 ms
B        129 ms          125-132 ms

PR description: "Leaderboard cache: p95 371 ms -> 129 ms (-65%), see k6 runs A and B."

Statement: "Runs A and B show that the cache flag cut the p95 of the leaderboard by about 65%."
questions.explanation: False. Run A started on cold pods and run B started on pods that run A had just warmed up, so the two whole-run numbers differ mostly by warm-up, not by the flag. Compared on their steady parts, both runs sit at about 125-131 ms: the evidence shows no measurable effect of the flag at all. The misconception is that the same script and rate make two runs comparable; they also need the same starting state, or the warm-up excluded from both, before any difference is attributed to the change.

challenges.name: exclude-the-warm-up
challenges.title: Exclude the warm-up, then compare two runs
challenges.description:
A pull request on CodeDev claims that a change made POST /api/submissions 40% faster at p95. The evidence is two recorded load test runs: the baseline ran right after a deploy on cold pods, the candidate on pods that were already warm. Write compare_runs(case) so that the comparison uses only the steady part of each run, with a warm-up rule that anyone can re-run and get the same answer.

Input (stdin, JSON): {"window_ms": W, "band": b, "baseline": samples, "candidate": samples}. Each sample is [t_ms, latency_ms]: t_ms is the time since the start of that run, latency_ms the response time. Samples can arrive in any order. W is a positive integer, 0 < b < 1.

Rule, applied to each run on its own:
1. A sample is valid when it is a list of exactly two numbers (int or float, not bool) with t_ms >= 0 and latency_ms > 0. Drop every other sample and count it in "dropped".
2. Put each valid sample in window floor(t_ms / W). Windows without samples are ignored. Compute the p95 of every non-empty window and list them in time order: V[0], ..., V[n-1].
3. Reference R = statistics.median(V[n // 2:]) (the median of the second half of the windows; the mean of the two middle values when that half has an even length).
4. The warm-up ends at the smallest index i such that every window from i to the end is inside the band: abs(V[j] - R) <= b * R for all j >= i. warmup_end_ms = (window number of V[i]) * W.
5. The steady state needs at least 3 windows (n - i >= 3). If there is no such i, or no valid sample at all, the run has no steady state: warmup_end_ms and p95 are null and every valid sample counts as excluded.
6. The steady samples are the valid samples with t_ms >= warmup_end_ms.

Percentiles (everywhere): nearest-rank on sorted samples, rank = ceil(p/100 * n), value = sorted[rank - 1]; an empty list has no percentile (null). The starter already has this percentile function.

Output (one JSON line): {"baseline": run, "candidate": run, "p95_change_pct": x, "naive_p95_change_pct": y}, where run = {"warmup_end_ms": int or null, "excluded": valid samples before warmup_end_ms, "steady_samples": count, "p95": p95 of the steady samples rounded with round(v, 1), or null, "dropped": count}.
- p95_change_pct = round((candidate p95 - baseline p95) / baseline p95 * 100, 1), using the unrounded p95 values; null when either run has no steady state.
- naive_p95_change_pct is the same formula on the p95 of all valid samples of each run (warm-up included), null when either run has no valid sample. It is the number the pull request reported.

Example: {"window_ms": 10000, "band": 0.2, "baseline": [...], "candidate": [...]} -> {"baseline": {"warmup_end_ms": 30000, "excluded": 60, "steady_samples": 100, "p95": 95.1, "dropped": 0}, "candidate": {...}, "p95_change_pct": -3.2, "naive_p95_change_pct": -68.5}.
hints: Take a run whose window p95 values are 410, 180, 240, 112, 108, 105, 110, 104. The second window is already close to the end value - so why can it not be the end of the warm-up?

Look at the order of the work: drop invalid samples first, then build the windows from valid samples only and skip empty windows, then take the reference from the second half of the window list, and only then search for the first window after which nothing leaves the band. Searching from the last window backwards is the easiest way to get "every later window" right. Check the 3-window minimum before you report a steady state.

A worked example with other numbers: window p95 values [600, 200, 130, 100, 104, 96, 101], band 0.1, W = 10000, no empty windows. n = 7, the second half is V[3:] = [100, 104, 96, 101], so R = 100.5 and the band is 90.45 to 110.55. From the end: 101, 96, 104, 100 are inside, 130 is not, so the steady state starts at index 3 with 4 windows (at least 3) and warmup_end_ms = 30000.

tests.name: Cold baseline vs warm candidate: the naive p95 change is mostly warm-up
A window that leaves the band again does not end the warm-up
Long warm-up: the reference comes from the second half of the windows only
Latency that keeps growing (a leak) never reaches a steady state: no comparison
Only two steady windows at the end are too short to compare
Invalid samples are dropped, empty windows ignored, input order does not matter
A run with no valid samples gives no steady state and no comparison
Large input: two 2,000-sample runs in 5 s windows
